name: Tomas Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Fenwick's, down the valley past the old mill. Dale Fenwick's got forty acres of apples and pears, about two hundred sheep that graze under the trees in winter, and barley on the top fields. Right now it's pruning, so I'm up a ladder with loppers from eight till it's dark. I sold feed to farmers for sixteen years before this. I knew every farm in the county from the kitchen table. Two years ago I decided I wanted to know one from the mud.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real. In sales, you never quite know if you did any good. Here, the tree either fruits or it doesn't. What wears me out is that I'm bad at pruning. Dale cuts a tree in ten minutes and it looks like a wine glass. Mine look like they've been in a fight. I've got an app that shows me where to cut from a photo, and Dale thinks it's cheating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, then the farms that use it well get a small edge and the rest carry on. That's how it went with every new feed and every new tractor I ever sold. I'd say it online, in the farming forum I'm on, without much fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed. I'd hoped it would make a small farm like Dale's cheaper to run, because I want to buy it when he retires. A plateau means I have to do it the old, expensive way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Keep using the AI every day for spray timing, pruning photos, pricing at the market. Keep saving hard, because I want the deposit for Fenwick's in about four years. Learn from Dale everything the app can't tell me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat. Like a sale that went fine but not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want to buy Fenwick's. Does Dale know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He knows. He's sixty-eight and his kids live in cities. We've talked about it over tea. He'd rather sell to someone local who'll keep the old trees than to a developer. That's me, if I can find the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Carmen agree with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carmen does the books for three small firms, part-time. She agrees, but she wants the numbers first. She's the one who'll say no if it doesn't add up. That's why we're married.

S0.say: I'd say the farms that use it well get a small edge and the rest carry on, like with every feed and tractor I ever sold. I'd post that on my farming forum without fuss.
S0.think: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, because I hoped AI would make a small farm like Dale's cheaper to run. I want to buy it when he retires, and a plateau means doing it the expensive way.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily for spray timing, pruning and market pricing. Saves hard towards a deposit on Fenwick's in about four years and learns everything the app can't teach from Dale.
S0.quote: He'd rather sell to someone local who'll keep the old trees than to a developer. That's me, if I can find the money.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is a former feed salesman with a clear goal: to buy the orchard farm he works on when its owner retires. He uses AI daily and is disappointed that a plateau doesn't make small farms cheaper. His wife's caution about numbers is part of the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for farming. We've been short of hands for twenty years. Let the machines do the ladders and the sprays, and let people do the thinking. I'd say it on the forum and I'd say it to Dale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's my chance. If a picking robot and a spray drone make forty acres work with one man instead of five, then I can afford Fenwick's. I'd feel a bit bad about the seasonal pickers, but that's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Dale about bringing the sale forward and doing a few trials now, a spray drone for this summer, maybe a pruning robot when they've been proven on a big orchard. I'd use AI to plan the whole business. I'd go to the bank with Carmen's numbers in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly. Like walking into a farm where I knew I'd get the order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel a bit bad about the pickers. Who are they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the same crew every September, families who travel for the harvest. Some have come to Fenwick's for fifteen years. I'd keep a few on, for the fruit that needs a person's eye. But not all. I'd be lying if I said all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about you, still learning? Doesn't the robot replace you too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It replaces the part of me that's bad at pruning. Good. What it doesn't replace is the man who owns the farm and decides what to grow. That's the job I'm after.

S1.say: I'd say this is good for farming after twenty years of labour shortages: let machines do the ladders and sprays and let people do the thinking. I'd say it online and to Dale.
S1.think: Privately it's my chance, because if robots make forty acres work with one man instead of five, I can afford Fenwick's. I'd feel bad for the seasonal pickers, but that's business.
S1.do: Asks Dale about bringing the sale forward and trials a spray drone this summer, with a pruning robot once proven. Uses AI to plan the business and goes to the bank with his wife's figures in the first year.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, like walking into a sale he knew he'd win.
S1.quote: It replaces the part of me that's bad at pruning. Good.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks to him like the key that makes buying the farm affordable. He's openly business-minded about the seasonal picking crew but honest that he wouldn't keep them all. He's after ownership, not his current job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge chance, but too fast for most people, and that families and churches will have to carry a lot of folk for a while. I wouldn't want the government taking over farms. I'd say hold on, adapt, help your neighbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years makes me nervous about buying. If AGI runs farms, land prices could do anything, and who knows what apples sell for when half the town's out of work. I'd still want the farm, but I'd be scared of buying at the wrong moment with all our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not rush the purchase. I'd ask Dale for a lease instead, so I run Fenwick's with robots and keep our savings safe. I'd use my old sales contacts to help other small farms set up the new kit, for a fee, because I know them all. And I'd keep the kids' college fund untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited and nervous at once. Like a big deal that could go either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said half the town could be out of work. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother. He drives a delivery van. And the pickers, again. Our parish has a food bank, I'd give time to that. Lucas could help too, he's fourteen, it'd do him good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you like risk. Why not just buy now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because liking risk isn't the same as being a fool. In sales I learned you don't sign when the customer is panicking. In two years, everyone's panicking. I'd wait for the dust.

S2.say: I'd say it's a huge chance but too fast for most people, and families and churches will have to carry many folk for a while. I'd tell people to hold on, adapt and help their neighbour, not let government take over farms.
S2.think: Two years makes me nervous about buying, because land and apple prices could do anything if half the town is out of work. I'd still want the farm but fear putting all our savings in at the wrong moment.
S2.do: Asks Dale for a lease instead of buying, so he can run the farm with robots and keep savings safe. Sets up as a paid adviser helping small farms he knows install new kit, and leaves the children's college fund untouched.
S2.feel: Uneasy, excited and nervous at once.
S2.quote: Because liking risk isn't the same as being a fool.
S2.fieldNote: Even an adaptive, risk-friendly person holds back when the change comes this fast, and he explains why using a lesson from sales. He swaps buying for leasing and adds a side income advising other farms. His worry turns to his brother, the pickers and his parish food bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the sweet spot. Enough time to plan, not so long that people get lazy. I'd tell every farmer I know: start trialling now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd buy Fenwick's. Dale retires on time, I set it up for the robots from day one, and by the time full AGI comes I own the land. I think owning things matters more, not less, when machines do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the bank meeting in the first six months. I'd put in the deposit, about forty percent of our savings, and keep the rest. I'd trial the drone and a picking robot in year two. I'd start Lucas on a part-time ag course so he learns the machines with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy. Like I'm finally doing what I came for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said owning things matters more. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a robot does the work, the person who owns the robot and the land gets paid. The person who only had their hands doesn't. I'd rather be the owner. That's not greed, it's looking after my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Debt. If I borrow for the farm and prices crash in year four, Carmen and I are stuck. She'd make me keep a big cushion. I'd let her.

S3.say: I'd say five years is the sweet spot, enough time to plan but not long enough for people to get lazy. I'd tell every farmer I know to start trials now.
S3.think: With five years I'd buy Fenwick's and set it up for robots from day one, so I own the land when full AGI arrives. Owning things matters more, not less, when machines do the work.
S3.do: Meets the bank within six months and puts about forty percent of savings into a deposit. Trials a spray drone and picking robot in year two and starts his son on a part-time agricultural course.
S3.feel: Calm and busy, finally doing what he came for.
S3.quote: If a robot does the work, the person who owns the robot and the land gets paid. The person who only had their hands doesn't.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is the timeline where his plan works best, and he'd buy the farm. His thinking is about ownership as protection for his family, and he denies it's greed. He accepts his wife's insistence on keeping a big cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse. Learn the tools, get your kids into the right trades, and look after each other. I wouldn't wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd buy Fenwick's on Dale's timeline, run it the old way for a few years while I learn properly, then bring in robots as they get cheap. By fifty-three I'd own a farm that runs itself mostly. I think that's a good life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the bank meeting in year two, not year one, because I'd want to learn more from Dale first. I'd keep saving and use AI for everything. I'd sit down with Lucas and Sofia about their plans, because ten years is exactly when they'd start working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd run it the old way first. Why, if you like new tech?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to know what a good tree looks like without the app. If I own it, I need to know when the robot is wrong. Dale's the only person who can teach me that, and he won't be around forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucas and Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucas, learn the machines and the land, and one day this is yours if you want it. Sofia wants to be a doctor. I'd say go for it, and learn the AI, because the doctors who use it will beat the ones who don't.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse: learn the tools, get your kids into the right trades and look after each other, without waiting for government.
S4.think: With ten years I'd buy Fenwick's on Dale's timeline, run it the old way while I learn, then bring in robots as they get cheap. By fifty-three I'd own a farm that mostly runs itself, and that's a good life.
S4.do: Delays the bank meeting to year two to learn more from Dale first, keeps saving and uses AI for everything. Talks with Lucas and Sofia about their plans, since they'd start work within the decade.
S4.quote: If I own it, I need to know when the robot is wrong.
S4.fieldNote: With the longest timeline he chooses to learn the old skills first, so he can tell when a robot is wrong. He's hopeful and sees a good life ahead. He'd encourage both children to master AI in their own fields.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's too fast to buy anything sensibly, and people I love would get hurt before they could adjust. What would help is banks willing to lend to small farms for new kit at fair rates, and apprenticeships so young people learn the machines on real farms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the robots. Everyone asks who loses their job. Nobody asks who'll own the machines that took it. I'd want it to be families like mine, not a few companies in a city.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks who'll own the machines that took it. I'd want it to be families like mine, not a few companies in a city.
portrait: Tomas Garcia is 43, a former feed salesman two years into work on an apple, pear and sheep farm whose owner he hopes to buy out when he retires. He uses AI every day, is still clumsy at pruning, and sees robots as the thing that could make a small farm affordable for him. He leans to free markets and family, and believes owning land and machines will matter more, not less. He's calm and even excited in most scenarios, holding back only when AGI comes in two years, when he'd lease rather than buy and worry for his brother and the seasonal pickers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would be too fast to buy the farm sensibly and people he loves would be hurt before they could adjust.
whatWouldHelp: Banks willing to lend small farms money for new equipment at fair rates, and apprenticeships so young people learn the machines on real farms.
